idea: Use the `tiktoken` encoder to count the tokens in each document in `docs` and calculate their 'quality' based on how many tokens they share in common with the `target_sample` documents (using a simple keyword/overlap or frequency approach, or simply prioritizing documents that have a higher ratio of unique tokens to total length).
why: Prioritizing documents that share a higher lexical overlap with the target domain will likely reduce the bits per byte on the held-out target set.
outcome: dev 1.9760 against 1.9611 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Calculate the token length of every document in `docs` and the `target_sample`. Prioritize documents that have a high ratio of shared 'content' tokens (non-stopword, non-punctuation) with the `target_sample` using a Jaccard similarity-like approach, while filtering out extremely short or purely junk (repetitive/low-entropy) strings.
why: The target sample consists of encyclopedic/informative text (Wikipedia-style), and prioritizing documents with similar vocabulary and structural characteristics should lower the bits per byte (bpb) more effectively than random selection.
outcome: dev 1.9798 against 1.9611 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Use tiktoken to encode the documents and select documents that have the highest density of unique 'content' tokens (excluding common stop words) that also appear frequently in the target_sample, while discarding documents that are shorter than 100 tokens or have a high ratio of non-alphanumeric characters.
why: The target sample consists of structured encyclopedic-style content; filtering for high-density, non-junk text that shares a vocabulary with the target domain should improve the model's ability to learn the specific style and facts required.
outcome: dev 1.9669 against 1.9611 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Replace the vocabulary-overlap scoring with a word-order-sensitive classifier, plus deduplication.

1. Dedupe: keep only the first occurrence of each document, keyed by a hash of the whitespace-normalised, lowercased text; also drop any document whose first 200 characters match one already kept.

2. Features: HashingVectorizer(analyzer='word', ngram_range=(1,2), token_pattern=r'\S+', lowercase=False, n_features=2**20, binary=True, norm='l2'), computed on the first 3000 characters of each document. Word bigrams over whitespace tokens capture the wikitext style (' @-@ ', ' , ', '= Title =') and penalise the word-shuffled and letter-scrambled documents, which unigram overlap cannot do.

3. Round 1 (positive vs unlabeled): positives are the 200 target_sample documents split into ~3000-character chunks; negatives are 4000 pool documents drawn with the CURATE_SEED rng. Fit LogisticRegression(C=10, class_weight='balanced', max_iter=300) and score every pool document.

4. Round 2 (self-training): refit with the top 15% of pool documents plus the target chunks as positives and the bottom 50% as negatives, then rescore.

5. Word-order check: build the set of word bigrams in target_sample and compute, per document, the fraction of its bigrams (first 3000 characters) found in that set. Push any document whose fraction is below half the median fraction of the round-2 positives to the bottom of the ranking.

6. Selection: count tokens with tiktoken gpt2. Take the deduped documents with round-2 probability > 0.5. If they hold fewer than T tokens, add further documents in descending score order until T is reached, so the fill is the next most similar clean prose and never spam, code or scrambled text. If they hold more than T, keep the highest-scoring T tokens.

7. Order: shuffle the selected indices with random.Random(CURATE_SEED) and return them.
why: The three rejected attempts all scored by token overlap, which cannot tell real target-style articles from the word-shuffled copies and wiki-word spam visible in the pool sample; a bigram classifier with deduplication should remove those while filling the whole T budget with in-domain or near-domain clean text.
outcome: dev 1.9455 against 1.9611 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: Replace the LogisticRegression classifier with a simple yet effective BM25-inspired scoring system. Use the target_sample to build a 'corpus' of terms (filtering out common stop words using a set), then score each pool document based on the frequency and recency of those terms within the first 3000 characters, combined with a penalty for very high 'garbage' character ratios (non-alphanumeric count > 20%).
why: The current LogisticRegression might overfit to noise in the small 200-doc target sample; a frequency-based approach with a junk-filtering heuristic is often more robust for identifying high-quality prose in noisy datasets.
outcome: dev 1.9795 against 1.9455 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Replace the LogisticRegression classifier with a 'Mutual Information' style score: for each document, calculate the ratio of bigrams that appear in both the target_sample and the document itself, normalized by the document's total bigram count, and use this to rank documents while maintaining the existing deduplication and word-order flag.
why: A direct overlap score (Mutual Information/Jaccard variant) on bigrams may be more robust than a LogisticRegression model trained on a small number of positive samples when the target domain is specific and the pool is large.
outcome: dev 1.9614 against 1.9455 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Replace the LogisticRegression classifier with a 'Pointwise' Cross-Encoder approach using a lightweight Cosine Similarity on the TF-IDF/Hashing vectors of the target_sample chunks vs. the pool documents, while incorporating a 'Density Score' that rewards documents with a high ratio of unique, high-frequency target tokens to total token count.
why: A pointwise similarity score combined with a density check can more accurately capture the thematic relevance of target documents than a linear classifier, which may struggle with the sparse, high-dimensional nature of the 2**20 feature space.
outcome: dev 1.9733 against 1.9455 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Keep dedupe, features, both classifier rounds and the bigram word-order flag unchanged. Change only step 6 (selection) so the gap is no longer filled with out-of-domain text, and add a typo filter.

1. Typo/damage rate. Over the deduped pool (first 3000 chars, lowercased alphabetic words of length >= 4), compute each word's document frequency. A word is 'rare' if it appears in fewer than 3 pool documents and is not in the target_sample vocabulary. Per document, rate = rare words / counted words. Call the confident set C0 = documents with p2 > 0.5 that are not flagged by the bigram check. Let med and MAD be the median and median absolute deviation of rate over C0. Mark a document 'damaged' if rate > med + 3*MAD. This targets character-corrupted wiki copies such as 'Ottawa Senatos' / 'ounded'.

2. Confident set C = C0 minus damaged documents, sorted by p2 descending. Count gpt2 tokens with tiktoken; call the total S.

3. Selection:
- If S >= T: keep the highest-p2 documents of C up to T tokens (as now).
- If 0.35*T <= S < T: return only C, shuffled once with random.Random(CURATE_SEED), and let the trainer cycle it. No filler.
- If S < 0.35*T: extend C down the ranking (undamaged, unflagged first; then damaged) until it holds 0.35*T tokens, then return that and let it cycle.

4. Order: seeded shuffle of the returned list, as now.
why: A 300-step from-scratch model is far from memorising, so repeating clean in-domain wikitext should match the held-out distribution better than spending part of the T-token budget on news/Q&A filler or typo-corrupted articles.
outcome: dev 1.8394 against 1.9455 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: Instead of just a bigram set for the word-order check, compute a small dense representation of the target_sample (e.g., using a mean of TF-IDF weighted vectors or a simple frequency-weighted unigram vector) and score the pool documents by their cosine similarity to this centroid, then use the existing logic to filter and select from this ranked list.
why: A centroid-based similarity provides a smoother global prior on the target domain's semantic distribution than a hard bigram match, potentially capturing more relevant documents with better stylistic alignment.
outcome: dev 1.8507 against 1.8394 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Replace the LogisticRegression-based scoring with a Cross-Encoder style approach where we compute the cosine similarity between each pool document's HashingVectorizer vector and the centroid of the target_sample chunks, while keeping the word-order bigram flag, typo filter, and selection logic (S >= T, 0.35T <= S < T, S < 0.35T) intact.
why: The current LogisticRegression model might overfit to noise in the 4000 random negatives; a centroid-based cosine similarity captures the global distribution of the target domain more robustly.
outcome: dev 1.8418 against 1.8394 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Modify the word-order check to use a smaller sliding window of bigrams (instead of all bigrams in the first 3000 chars) and switch the bigram matching from a set-based inclusion to a weighted overlap, where the weight of a bigram is its frequency in the target_sample. Also, increase the rarity threshold for the typo filter to 5 to be less aggressive on niche but valid vocabulary.
why: A weighted bigram overlap better captures the 'style' of the target domain (like Wikipedia's specific phrasing) than a binary check, while a slightly higher rarity threshold prevents the typo filter from over-penalizing valid, domain-specific technical terms.
outcome: dev 1.8446 against 1.8394 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Keep everything up to and including the confident set C (step 6b) unchanged, then add one self-consistency purge over the FULL text of each document in C before selection. The current damage checks only see the first 3000 characters and only compare against the 200-document target sample.

1. Tokenise the full text of every document in C with str.split(). Map words to integer ids and encode each word bigram as id1*V+id2.

2. Compute the document frequency of each bigram over C (count once per document). A bigram is 'supported' if its document frequency is >= 2, i.e. it also occurs in at least one other C document (leave-one-out).

3. Cut each document into consecutive windows of 400 words. Merge a final window shorter than 100 words into the previous one. For each window compute coverage = supported bigrams / bigrams.

4. Let med and MAD be the median and median absolute deviation of coverage over all windows of C (if MAD is 0, use the mean absolute deviation). Remove a document from C if either:
- any of its windows has coverage < med - 4*MAD, or
- its whole-document coverage < med - 3*MAD.
This catches documents that are shuffled or character-corrupted only after the head, lightly corrupted or locally shuffled documents that pass the head-only checks, and stray non-wiki text glued into a document.

5. Safety: if the purge would remove more than 30% of C's documents, loosen it to remove only the 30% with the lowest minimum-window coverage.

6. Run the existing selection on the purged C exactly as now: top-p2 documents up to T; cycle if S >= 0.35*T; otherwise extend down the ranking to the 0.35*T floor, with purged documents going last, alongside the 'damaged' tier. Finish with the same seeded shuffle.

Use plain dict/Counter on integer keys so the pass stays within a few tens of seconds.
why: The biggest gain so far came from removing damaged wiki copies, and the remaining contamination is most likely damage that the head-only, 200-document checks cannot see, which a full-text leave-one-out bigram check against the much larger confident set should detect.
outcome: dev 1.8273 against 1.8394 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best
